claims.text: Group IV-containing RHEA hydride powders have high internal strain and surface area and are susceptible to rapid oxidation during heating.
Cold pressing hydride powder in a sealed, evacuated extrusion die followed by immediate hot extrusion can avoid ambient oxygen exposure.
Heating to 400°C at 5°C/min under 10^-4 Pa will initiate hydride decomposition and hydrogen desorption.
A rapid ramp to 0.85 T_melt, followed by a 30-minute hold under 10^-7 Pa, is an appropriate high-temperature consolidation history.
The oxygen partial pressure must remain below 10^-10 Pa throughout processing.
The proposed vacuum thermal history will suppress oxygen uptake and diffusion into the alloy.
Suppressing oxygen uptake will inhibit nucleation and growth of a brittle alpha-HCP phase.
The process will retain a single-phase metastable BCC solid solution.
Rapid low-temperature hydrogen removal prevents oxygen-stabilized surface oxides that would nucleate alpha-HCP.
The ultra-high-vacuum high-temperature hold facilitates solid-state sintering and dynamic recrystallization of the BCC phase.
An extremely low oxygen partial pressure thermodynamically disfavors stable oxide formation.
Low oxygen availability kinetically suppresses oxygen diffusion required for an HCP transformation.
Extrusion pressure provides densification without prolonged high-temperature exposure that would permit oxygen ingress.
The resulting bulk will reach greater than 98% of theoretical density.
The resulting bulk will exhibit no catastrophic cracking.
The resulting alloy will have a ductile-to-brittle transition temperature below room temperature.
The processed alloy will have 20–30% higher yield strength at 1000°C than conventionally processed alloys.
Retention of a fine-grained BCC structure contributes to increased strength.
Conventional inert-gas or air decomposition, sintering, and extrusion typically cause oxygen uptake, alpha-HCP precipitation, increased transition temperature, and extrusion cracking.
The proposed method is specifically applicable to hydride-derived RHEAs with significant Zr, Hf, or Ti content and not to alloys whose target phase is inherently HCP.
